newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish treasury sees T-bill yields up, bonds flat.
newsitem.headline: Polish treasury sees T-bill yields up, bonds flat.

text.p: Polish T-bill prices may fall at upcoming tenders, but bond prices are likely to hold steady, a senior finance ministry official said.
"Low demand (at recent auctions) has become troublesome, and we must increase T-bill yields," Arkadiusz Kaminski, deputy head of the Public Debt Department, told Reuters.
Kaminski said, however, that treasury yields would not reach levels of comparable central bank NBP-bills because such a move would place to large a burden on deficit financing costs.

"We painfully feel the difference between yields on T-bills and NBP-bills, but we will not be able to drive T-bill yields so high because this would increase the cost of financing the budget deficit by too much," Kaminski said.

At Monday's primary T-bill auction, all minimum prices fell with the deepest 0.26-point minimum price cut noted in the benchmark 52-week paper, whose maximum yield jumped to 20.40 percent from 20.03 percent.
The central bank has been selling its NBP-bills at a flat yield curve of 22 percent from 91- to 273-days.
Kaminski also said the Polish treasury did not expect any significant rise in bond yields in the near future because those yields were already more attractive than T-bill rates.
"I don't expect any significant increase in bond yields as they are already better than T-bill yields," he said.
At the last fixed bond tender earlier this month, 15-percent two-year bonds were sold with a maximum yield of 20.6 percent and 12-percent five-year bonds yielded 18.5 percent.
Poland also offers three-year floating rate bonds, whose interest is based on 13-week T-bill yields plus a interest margin and 10-year floaters based on the benchmark with a small interest margin.

Kaminski said that over the last two month budget financing needs have largely been met by successful bond auctions as demand for T-bills waned to a two-year low of 334 million zlotys at last Monday's one billion zloty primary tender.
"If bond sales were not succesfull... we would have been forced to increase T-bill yields earlier to meet large borrowing needs in the first quarter of 1997," he said.
Kaminski said Poland would strive to encourage investors to buy longer-term bonds because they spread-out the cost of financing the budget deficit over several years.
But analysts have said that many investors would likely refrain from entering the bond market until complicated secondary trading rules were cleared and liquidity increased.
